opus-5.5.text:
I think multi-agent is one of the most underexplored directions right now, and part of the reason is that the single-agent paradigm has been working so well. When you can keep scaling a single model and keep getting better results, there isn't a lot of pressure to look elsewhere. But I think that's going to change.

If you look at how humans accomplish really big things, it's almost never one person working alone. Civilization is fundamentally a multi-agent achievement. We have cooperation, competition, specialization, institutions, markets. A lot of human intelligence emerges from these interactions rather than from any individual brain. So I think there's a real question of whether AI can benefit from something analogous. Not just running a bunch of copies of the same model in parallel, but agents that actually interact, negotiate, build on each other's work, and maybe even develop something like culture over time.

My background is in games like poker and Diplomacy, and those taught me a lot about how different multi-agent settings are. In two-player zero-sum games you have nice theoretical guarantees and you can basically self-play your way to superhuman performance. But once you move into settings with cooperation, like Diplomacy, things get much messier. You can't just optimize in a vacuum, because you have to model and work with other agents, often humans, who have their own conventions and expectations. With Cicero we found that pure self-play would converge on strategies humans couldn't understand or coordinate with, so we had to ground the agent in human behavior.

So when I think about untapped potential, I think about two things. One is using multi-agent interaction to scale capabilities beyond what a single model thinking longer can achieve. The other is getting AI systems that work well alongside people and other AIs in the real world, which is inherently a multi-agent environment. I don't think we've cracked either yet, and I'd be surprised if there weren't big gains waiting there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think multi-agent is interesting because it's where a lot of my background comes from. I spent years working on poker and Diplomacy, and those are fundamentally multi-agent problems. And I think there's a pretty common misconception that multi-agent is going to be this huge unlock, that you just take a bunch of models and have them talk to each other and you get some emergent intelligence that's way beyond what any single model can do.

I'm actually a bit more skeptical of that framing than most people. A lot of the gains people attribute to multi-agent setups are really just gains from spending more inference compute. If you have ten agents debating a problem, you're using ten times the compute, and the question you should ask is whether that's better than having one model think ten times longer. And in a lot of cases, it isn't. The single model with more test-time compute often does just as well or better, and it's a much cleaner thing to scale.

That said, there are places where I think multi-agent is genuinely important, and it's not where people usually look. The first is when the environment itself is multi-agent, meaning there are other actors, humans or AIs, with their own goals, and you have to reason about what they're going to do. That's negotiation, that's markets, that's any situation where the right action depends on other agents' strategies. Diplomacy taught me a lot about how hard that is, because you can't just optimize for yourself in a vacuum. You have to model the other players, and in human-facing settings you have to model them as humans, not as perfectly rational agents. That's a very different problem from chess or Go.

The second is as a training signal. Self-play is a form of multi-agent learning, and it's arguably the most important idea behind AlphaGo and behind the poker work. The reason it worked is that the agent could generate its own curriculum by playing against itself, and the difficulty scaled automatically. The big open question is whether you can get something like that in domains that aren't zero-sum games. If you can set up environments where agents generate hard problems for each other and verify each other's answers, that's a path to improvement that doesn't bottleneck on human data. I think that's the version of multi-agent that's really untapped, and it's much less about orchestration and much more about where the learning signal comes from.

And then there's the longer-term thing, which is that eventually you're going to have a lot of these systems operating in the world at the same time, interacting with each other, and we don't really understand the dynamics of that yet. Game theory gives you some tools, but the classical theory assumes things about rationality and common knowledge that don't hold for these models. So I think there's real research to be done there, and it's somewhat under-explored because everyone is focused on making the single agent smarter. Which, to be fair, is still where most of the gains are coming from right now.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential, but the key question is where the benefit actually comes from. If you take a model and have ten copies of it discuss a problem, are you getting something that you couldn’t get by letting one copy think for ten times as long? I don’t think that’s obvious.

One promising direction is having agents explore different approaches independently and then check each other’s work. If they all share the same initial reasoning, they might all make the same mistake. But if they arrive at answers separately, comparing those answers could be useful—especially when checking a solution is easier than finding it.

And then there’s the question of agents interacting with people and with other agents that have different goals. Now you need to reason about what somebody else knows, what they want, and how they’re going to respond. That’s a different challenge from solving a problem in isolation. I think there’s a lot left to explore there, both in cooperation and in negotiation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of untapped potential, especially if you think of multi-agent AI as more than just having several models talk to each other. The interesting question is: how do you structure those interactions so that the group actually does better than a single model with the same computational budget?

You could have agents explore different approaches to a problem, critique one another’s assumptions, or bring different information to a decision. But if they all make the same mistake, or they just agree with whoever speaks first, you haven’t gained much. You need some way to evaluate the contributions and combine them effectively.

And then there’s the setting where agents have different objectives. They have to negotiate, cooperate, and reason about what another agent knows or intends. That’s a much richer problem than answering a question in isolation. I think games are a useful testing ground for that, because you can measure whether an agent’s reasoning actually leads to better outcomes. The exciting opportunity is to take those capabilities into settings where people and AI systems need to work together.
